title: SOS Signal Beacon
pitch: An LED that flashes the famous ··· ––– ··· distress signal in Morse code.

guide.about: Your first real circuit: one LED, one resistor, and code that turns timing into a message. You'll learn how digitalWrite() and delay() make lights blink.
steps: Push the LED into the breadboard. The long leg is +, the short leg (flat side of the rim) is −.
Put the 220Ω resistor so one end is in the same row as the LED's long leg.
Run a jumper wire from the resistor's other end to Pin 9 on the board.
Run a jumper wire from the LED's short leg row to a GND pin.
Plug in USB, paste the code into the Arduino IDE, choose your board and port, and press Upload.
Watch the LED: three short, three long, three short flashes, then a pause.
guide.test: The LED (and the board's own little LED) blinks ··· ––– ··· again and again. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 to see the letters print.
next: Change the message array to blink your name in Morse.
Add a second LED that lights during the pauses.

title: Mini Traffic Light
pitch: Red, yellow and green LEDs that cycle like a real crossroads, with an optional walk button.

guide.about: Build a working traffic light. If you add a button, pressing it makes the light switch to red sooner so a pedestrian can cross, just like real crossings.
wiring: no resistor needed: the code uses INPUT_PULLUP
steps: Place the three LEDs in a column: red on top, yellow, then green.
Give each LED its own 220Ω resistor from its long leg to a separate row.
Wire the resistors to pins 4 (red), 3 (yellow) and 2 (green).
Connect a GND pin to the breadboard's − rail and plug every LED short leg into that rail.
(Optional) Put the button across the middle gap of the breadboard. Wire one leg to Pin 7 and the diagonally opposite leg to GND.
Upload the code and watch the cycle: green → yellow → red → green.
guide.test: Green stays on 6 s, yellow 2 s, red 6 s. With the button: press it during green and the light goes yellow within a second.
next: Add a second set of LEDs for the crossing road.
Add a passive buzzer that ticks while pedestrians may walk.

title: Click-Click Lamp
pitch: Tap a button to switch a light on and off. Hold it to make the light breathe softly.

guide.about: Learn how to read a button properly, including "debouncing" (ignoring the tiny electrical bounces a button makes when pressed).
steps: Put the button across the breadboard's middle gap.
Wire one button leg to Pin 2 and the diagonally opposite leg to GND.
Add the LED with its 220Ω resistor between Pin 9 and the LED's long leg; short leg to GND.
Upload the code.
Tap the button to toggle the lamp. Hold it for 1 second to start breathing mode.
guide.test: A short tap toggles on/off. Holding for more than a second makes the LED fade in and out until you tap again.
next: Swap the LED for a WS2812B stick for a color lamp.
Add a potentiometer to set the brightness.

title: Reaction Speed Duel
pitch: Two players, two buttons. Wait for the light… whoever slaps their button first wins!

guide.about: A two-player reflex game. A light turns on after a random wait. Press too early and you lose the round! Results and reaction times show in the Serial Monitor.
parts: any colors: 1 GO light + 1 per player
three 220Ω for LEDs, one 220Ω for the buzzer
steps: Place the GO LED in the middle and one LED near each player's button.
Give every LED a 220Ω resistor and wire them to pins 9 (GO), 10 (P1) and 11 (P2). Short legs to GND.
Put the two buttons at opposite ends of the breadboard: P1 to Pin 2, P2 to Pin 3, other legs to GND.
(Optional) Connect the passive buzzer: + through a 220Ω resistor to Pin 8, − to GND.
Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Both players hold a finger near their button. When GO lights up, press!
guide.test: The winner's LED blinks and the Serial Monitor prints the reaction time in milliseconds. Press before GO and the other player wins the round.
next: Keep score to 5 and play a victory tune.
Show the times on an I2C LCD.

title: Auto Night Light
pitch: A light that wakes up by itself when the room gets dark and glows brighter the darker it gets.

guide.about: Use a photoresistor and a 10kΩ resistor as a "voltage divider" so the board can measure light. Then fade an LED using PWM (fast on/off switching that looks like dimming).
steps: Put the LDR in the breadboard. Its legs have no + or −.
Wire one LDR leg to 5V and the other leg's row to A0.
Add the 10kΩ resistor from that same A0 row to GND.
Add the LED with its 220Ω resistor on Pin 9, short leg to GND.
Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor at 9600 to see light readings.
Cover the LDR with your hand: the LED should fade on.
guide.test: In a bright room the LED is off. Cover the LDR and it glows; the darker it gets, the brighter it shines. If it never turns on, change DARK_LEVEL in the code to a value between your bright and dark readings.
next: Replace the LED with a WS2812B ring for a color night light.
Add a PIR sensor so it only lights when someone walks by.

title: Fridge Door Alarm
pitch: Left the fridge open? This little gadget notices the light inside and beeps after 20 seconds.

guide.about: The fridge light switches on when the door opens. The light sensor module's DO pin tells the board "bright" or "dark", and the board starts a timer. Too long open means beeping.
parts: the module with a blue adjustment knob
power from a power bank inside the fridge
steps: Wire the light module: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, DO to Pin 2.
Wire the buzzer: + through a 220Ω resistor to Pin 8, − to GND.
Upload the code, then power the board.
Calibrate: shine a light on the module and turn its blue knob until its small DO light turns ON in light and OFF when you cover it.
Open the Serial Monitor at 9600: it prints BRIGHT or DARK.
Test it with your phone flashlight, then place it in the fridge running from a power bank.
guide.test: Keep the module in light: after 20 seconds the buzzer beeps until it gets dark again. Cover it and the beeping stops at once.
safety: Keep the electronics in a small sealed bag or box: fridges are damp.
next: Change OPEN_LIMIT_MS for a shorter or longer limit.
Count how many times the door was opened today.

title: Pocket Jukebox
pitch: A buzzer that plays tunes. Press the button to switch songs, including an original "Lab Theme".

guide.about: Learn how tone() turns numbers into musical notes. The songs are stored as lists of notes and lengths, so you can write your own.
parts: a TTP223 touch pad also works
wiring: (touch module: SIG → Pin 2, VCC → 5V, GND → GND)
steps: Wire the buzzer + through the 220Ω resistor to Pin 8 and − to GND.
Wire the button between Pin 2 and GND.
If you use the TTP223 touch pad instead, set USE_TOUCH to true in the code.
Upload the code.
Press the button: the next song plays. Press during a song to skip.
guide.test: Each press plays the next tune: Lab Theme, Twinkle Twinkle, Ode to Joy, Happy Birthday.
next: Write your own melody in the songs table.
Put it in a small box powered by a USB power bank as a music-box gift.

title: Electronic Dice
pitch: Press a button: the 7-segment digit spins like a slot machine and lands on 1 to 6.

guide.about: Control all 7 segments of a digit yourself to draw numbers, and use random() for fair dice rolls. The spin animation slows down like a real die.
parts: seven 220Ω (one per segment) + one 220Ω for the buzzer
steps: Find pin 1 of the display: with the decimal point at the bottom right, pin 1 is bottom-left, pins go 1–5 along the bottom and 6–10 along the top (right to left).
Place the display across the breadboard gap.
Connect a 220Ω resistor from each segment pin, then a wire to the board pin from the table.
Connect display pin 3 (or 8: they're joined inside) to GND.
Wire the button between Pin 12 and GND. (Optional) Buzzer on Pin 11 with a 220Ω resistor.
Upload the code, then press the button to roll!
guide.test: At power-up all segments light for a moment, then the display shows a dash. Each press spins and lands on 1–6. If the digits look scrambled, two segment wires are swapped: check the pinout of your display's datasheet.
next: Add a second display for two dice.
Use a TM1637 display to show the total of several rolls.

title: Knob Dimmer
pitch: Turn a knob, and the light smoothly dims and brightens: your first analog-to-PWM project.

guide.about: Read a knob with analogRead() (0–1023) and set LED brightness with analogWrite() (0–255). This in → map → out pattern is used in tons of projects.
steps: Plug the potentiometer into the breadboard with its three legs in three different rows.
Wire outer legs to GND and 5V, and the middle leg to A0.
Add the LED and its 220Ω resistor to Pin 9, short leg to GND.
Upload the code and turn the knob.
guide.test: Turning the knob fully one way switches the LED off, the other way makes it full brightness. The Serial Monitor (9600) shows the numbers.
next: Control a servo's angle with the same knob.
Use the knob to set the speed of a blinking light.

title: Mood Lamp Color Wheel
pitch: Turn one knob to sweep an RGB LED through every color of the rainbow.

guide.about: Mix red, green and blue light with PWM to make any color. The code turns one knob position into a "hue" (position on the color wheel).
parts: common cathode: long leg goes to GND
steps: Find the RGB LED's longest leg: that's the common cathode. The order is usually red, common, green, blue.
Put the LED in the breadboard and connect the longest leg to GND.
Give each color leg its own 220Ω resistor, then wire red → 9, green → 10, blue → 11.
Wire the potentiometer: outer legs to 5V and GND, middle to A0.
Upload the code and turn the knob.
guide.test: The color sweeps red → yellow → green → cyan → blue → magenta as you turn. If red and green seem swapped, swap those two wires.
next: Put the LED under a frosted cup or a paper lantern.
Add a button that switches to an automatic rainbow mode.

title: Rainbow Fade Lamp
pitch: A common-anode RGB LED that drifts through soft rainbow colors. A button changes the speed.

guide.about: With a common-anode LED the shared leg goes to + and a color lights when its pin goes LOW, so the code "flips" every brightness value. A neat lesson in reading the variant!
parts: common anode: long leg goes to 5V
steps: Find the longest leg of the RGB LED and connect it to 5V (not GND!).
Put a 220Ω resistor on each color leg, then wire red → 9, green → 10, blue → 11.
Wire the button between Pin 2 and GND.
Upload the code.
Press the button to cycle through slow, medium and fast fading.
guide.test: The LED glides smoothly through the rainbow. If it's stuck on white or looks inverted, check that the long leg is on 5V.
next: Diffuse it with a ping-pong ball for a glowing orb.
Add a light sensor so it only runs at night.

title: Morse Code Messenger
pitch: Type a message on your PC and watch the board blink it out in Morse code. Just the board, nothing else!

guide.about: Uses only the board's built-in LED and the Serial Monitor. You'll learn how to read text sent from your computer and convert letters into Morse timing.
parts: one 220Ω, only if you add the buzzer
steps: Plug the board into your PC with the USB cable.
Paste the code into the Arduino IDE and upload it.
Open the Serial Monitor (top right) and set it to 9600 baud and "Newline".
Type a message like HELLO LAB and press Enter.
Watch the little LED marked L blink your message.
guide.test: The Serial Monitor echoes each letter as dots and dashes while the L LED blinks them.
next: Add an LED on Pin 9 for a bigger light.
Make the speed adjustable with a potentiometer.
